implementation_notes: The contract is a header plus a symbol map: all types the consumer needs are declared opaque or version-suffixed, every published entry point exists in a named symbol version, and the implementation lives behind them. New behaviour is added as additional symbols inside the same library rather than by changing an existing layout, which is how long-lived C libraries let years-old binaries keep running while the implementation moves on.
pitfalls: Struct-layout changes break the ABI even when the function signature is unchanged; keep published structs opaque or size-tagged and never reorder members.
Linking without the version script exports every helper symbol, turning internal functions into accidental protocol surface; keep --version-script in the build and mark the rest local.

variants.name: gRPC C core service from a .proto contract
variants.implementation_notes: When the consumers are remote, the protocol is a .proto and protoc generates the message types and the service scaffolding served by the gRPC C core; the handler translates generated request structs to internal domain calls, so the wire schema - not the C headers - is the published contract. Choose this when the subsystem is consumed across processes or languages; keep the ABI variant when consumers are linked code.
pitfalls: Generated C structs must be re-generated and the library re-released whenever the schema changes; a stale generated header is a silent contract mismatch.
The gRPC C core is built with a C++ toolchain, so the published C ABI now depends on build settings you do not control - pin them.
